query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, local chemical interactions drive nanoscale clustering (especially of Al‐rich regions) that is stabilized by high configurational entropy and sluggish atomic diffusion. Under conditions such as high-temperature compressive loading or irradiation, these clusters tend to rearrange into a short‐range ordered state, which in turn suppresses unwanted phase separations (precipitation), promotes the formation of protective oxide scales, and reinforces defect blocking. This combined effect governs phase stability and is responsible for concurrently retaining high-temperature strength, excellent environmental resistance, enhanced radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, disordered FCC A1 state (e.g., Al0.1CrCoFeNi) with a statistically random distribution of elements.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled external stimulus—such as high-temperature compressive strain or controlled ion irradiation—to activate atomic rearrangements that enhance local ordering (clustering-to-ordering transition).
generation.conditions: Tests should be conducted over temperature regimes that include high-temperature conditions (for oxidation and strength tests), irradiation conditions (to assess radiation tolerance), and cryogenic temperatures (for toughness evaluation) compared against an unstimulated baseline.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical clusters enriched in Al (and correlated with its affinity with Ni) that rearrange under stimuli into short-range order, thereby augmenting local energy barriers for deleterious transformations.
generation.mechanism: Negative mixing enthalpies between like species (especially Al–Al and Al–Ni) and atomic size mismatches promote local clustering. The high configurational entropy and sluggish atomic diffusion kinetically restrain complete phase segregation, allowing a metastable disordered matrix. Under compressive or irradiation conditions, clusters rearrange into an ordered pattern that retards precipitation, enhances the formation of protective oxide scales (through Al/Cr segregation at the surface), and stabilizes fault structures that improve cryogenic plasticity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline processed without the additional stimulus, alloys that undergo the clustering-to-ordering transition will exhibit a reduced tendency for radiation-induced precipitation, lower oxidation mass gain at high temperature (due to more uniformly protective oxide layers), and maintain or enhance cryogenic toughness due to improved intrinsic deformation mechanisms.
generation.baseline: Identical Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy samples processed under standard conditions (without induced compressive loading or controlled irradiation) that maintain a statistically random solid-solution microstructure.
generation.boundary: This mechanism applies to single-phase, equiatomic or near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys (e.g., with low Al content such as x ≈ 0.1 in AlxCrCoFeNi) where clustering is predominant; it may not hold in multiphase compositions (e.g., those showing B2, σ, or other intermetallic phases) or under processing conditions that override the influence of local chemical interactions.
generation.uncertainty: While molecular-dynamics studies (PMC4976365) and irradiation experiments (PMC4999872) support the existence of clustering and the benefits of high configurational entropy/sluggish diffusion on suppressing precipitation, the direct quantitative links to oxidation behavior and cryogenic toughness in operational environments remain to be fully established. The interplay between induced short-range order and its impact on multiple performance metrics requires further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al0.1CrCoFeNi samples: one set is pre-conditioned by applying a controlled high-temperature compressive strain (or low-fluence ion irradiation) to promote the clustering-to-ordering transition, while the control set is processed under standard conditions. Subject both sets to high-temperature oxidation tests, controlled ion irradiation (to induce potential precipitation), and cryogenic tensile testing. Microstructure evolution should be characterized using TEM and XRD and analyzed via pair-distribution functions.
measurements: Oxidation mass gain over a fixed duration at high temperatures
Density and size distribution of irradiation-induced precipitates
Tensile strength, ductility, and fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures
Degree of local order measured via pair correlations from TEM or atom probe
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-conditioned samples do not show statistically significant improvements (i.e., lower precipitation, more protective oxide formation, and enhanced cryogenic mechanical properties) compared to the control samples, or if similar improvements occur without the induced clustering-to-ordering transition, then the hypothesis—that local clustering and its stress- or irradiation-induced ordering govern phase stability and the desirable multi-environment performance—would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study AlxCrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. In contrast, the configurational entropy of single phase HEA Al0.1CoCrFeNi is much higher, which competes with the positive mixing enthalpy in the ion irradiation and reduces the thermodynamic driving force for precipitation. Furthermore, due to the high configurational entropy the thermodynamic stability of single phase Al0.1CoCrFeNi is increased with temperature increasing, enhancing the stability of random solid solution during the evolution of high energy displacement cascades induced by ion irradiation. Another reason for the great resistance of single phase HEA to precipitation may be the sluggish atomic diffusion. The formation of precipitates in the ion irradiation is attributed to the fluxes of irradiation-induced defects, the defect fluxes towards various sinks result in the solute depletion or segregation at sinks.
